metadata.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says she hasn’t ruled out a potential run for president or Senate in 2028

sources.news_title: Democrat Ocasio-Cortez Does Not Rule Out Seeking the U.S. Presidency in 2028
sources.text:
Política
La demócrata Ocasio-Cortez no descarta buscar la Presidencia de EE UU en 2028
Ocasio-Cortez es considerada una heredera política del senador Bernie Sanders, exaspirante a la candidatura presidencial demócrata, y mantiene una estrecha relación política con el alcalde de Nueva York, Zohran Mamdani, vinculado a la corriente de socialistas democráticos del partido
La congresista demócrata Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, una de las principales figuras del ala izquierdista del partido, afirmó este domingo que no descarta presentarse a las elecciones presidenciales de 2028 para suceder al mandatario republicano, Donald Trump.
Ocasio-Cortez, de origen puertorriqueño, hizo esas declaraciones en una entrevista con la cadena ABC al ser preguntada por una reciente encuesta de la Universidad de Nuevo Hampshire que la sitúa como favorita en las primarias presidenciales demócratas.
"No he descartado la posibilidad y me siento muy honrada por el enorme apoyo que recibo", respondió la congresista, de 36 años, quien, no obstante, aseguró que ahora está "concentrada" en lograr su reelección por su distrito de Nueva York en las elecciones de medio mandato del próximo 3 de noviembre.
Durante la entrevista, Ocasio-Cortez tampoco descartó competir en las primarias demócratas contra el líder de los demócratas en el Senado, Chuck Schumer, para intentar arrebatarle su escaño por Nueva York en 2028.
A su juicio, la reciente victoria de Abdul El-Sayed en las primarias demócratas para el Senado demuestra que el partido está experimentando una "renovación" generacional.
El-Sayed, musulmán y situado en el ala izquierdista del partido, se impuso el martes en las primarias para ocupar un escaño por Míchigan y ha sido criticado por Trump y los republicanos, que consideran que los demócratas están abrazando el comunismo.
Ocasio-Cortez es considerada una heredera política del senador Bernie Sanders, exaspirante a la candidatura presidencial demócrata, y mantiene una estrecha relación política con el alcalde de Nueva York, Zohran Mamdani, vinculado a la corriente de socialistas democráticos del partido.
La encuesta de la Universidad de Nuevo Hampshire sobre las primarias presidenciales demócratas sitúa a Ocasio-Cortez al frente, con un 22 % de los apoyos, seguida del exsecretario de Transporte Pete Buttigieg, con un 21 %, y del gobernador de California, Gavin Newsom, con un 15 %.
En el bando republicano, los favoritos para suceder a Trump, quien no puede optar a un tercer mandato, son el vicepresidente, JD Vance, y el secretario de Estado, Marco Rubio.

sources.news_title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says she hasn’t ruled out a potential run for president or Senate in 2028
sources.text:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., said Sunday that she hasn’t ruled out a potential run for president or the Senate 2028, echoing remarks she’s made while campaigning for congressional candidates ahead of November’s midterm elections.
“I’m focused on winning the midterms. I’m running for Congress right now,” Ocasio-Cortez first told ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday when asked whether she plans to run for president in two years.
Pressed further by “This Week” host Jonathan Karl, Ocasio-Cortez added, “I haven’t ruled out the possibility. And I’m very humbled to the tremendous amount of support out there.” But she reiterated her focus on the upcoming midterms over her own political future.
Asked whether she’d consider running for the Senate in New York in 2028, when Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., will be up for re-election, Ocasio-Cortez, 36, answered, “I think that anything is possible at this juncture.”
The congresswoman’s political future has been the subject of speculation for years as she’s wielded her national political power to endorse insurgent progressive candidates who have beaten more moderate, establishment candidates with bigger campaign war chests.
Most recently, Abdul El-Sayed, a candidate who pledged to reject funding for Israel and promote “Medicare for All,” beat Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., in the Great Lakes State’s Democratic primary for Senate last week, overcoming the tens of millions of dollars spent by Stevens’ supporters to attack him.
“I think that we are in a time of renewal for the Democratic Party. And it’s tremendously exciting for all of us, for the big tent of the Democratic Party,” Ocasio-Cortez said Sunday in the wake of El-Sayed’s victory. “We have really an ascendance of a young, inspiring, exciting electorate, energizing wave of candidates that I think really inject a new energy to the Democratic Party and add to the toolbox of candidates that we have to win the midterm elections hopefully in November.”
El-Sayed’s victory was fueled in part by Ocasio-Cortez’s endorsement and by the backing of Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who ran for president twice as a progressive, anti-establishment alternative to traditional Democrats.
Sanders has all but ruled out another presidential run in 2028, drawing questions about who might take up the mantle of the movement he began in 2016.
Ocasio-Cortez, to some, appears to be a natural successor, especially as she and Sanders crisscrossed the nation together since the last presidential election, urging supporters to fight oligarchy and support Medicare for All.
In July, while campaigning for El-Sayed in Michigan, the congresswoman told Politico when asked about a presidential run: “I mean, I can’t say that I’ve ruled it out.”
She was first elected to Congress in 2018, winning her party’s nomination for New York’s 14th Congressional District in a shocking upset to the Queens machine after she challenged longtime Rep. David Crowley in the Democratic primary.
On Sunday, Ocasio-Cortez reflected on her political rise since 2018, telling Karl:
“It has been the greatest privilege of my life to be able to represent the working people of my congressional district. And I think some of the ways that it’s changed me has been to be able to come in with so many aspirations for our country, and then to have the remarkable opportunity to be in the arena and try to make the country a better place, challenges and all.”
“And I love that it’s hard,” she added. “I love that I have to and I get to engage with people from all across the country, elected officials from all across the country, to try to actually fulfill our dreams to guarantee healthcare to every American.”
The congresswoman also spoke about a personal milestone she revealed on Instagram last week — freezing her eggs — and why she decided to publicly share such a personal decision.
On Saturday, Ocasio-Cortez posted videos of herself on Instagram administering the first injections in the egg-freezing process. “I want to share this because I’ve been weighing this for a very long time … and there isn’t a lot out there, and sometimes it can feel very daunting,” she said in her posts from Saturday night.
Asked by Karl about the decision, Ocasio-Cortez said: “In this political environment where this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy, I think it’s important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes, especially for working women across the country, and normalize them.”

sources.news_title: AOC Says She Hasn’t “Ruled Out the Possibility” of 2028 Presidential Run or Primary Against Chuck Schumer
sources.text:
Firebrand socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) said nothing is off the table in 2028 during an interview with ABC’s Jonathan Karl on Sunday.
“I’m focused on winning the midterms. I’m running for Congress right now,” she said while leaving the door open to a presidential bid or a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.
This comes as AOC leads the Democratic field in New Hampshire, historically the first in the nation.
Asked if a 2028 presidential run was “realistic,” AOC said, “Well, I haven’t ruled out the possibility.”
On a 2028 primary against Chuck Schumer, she said, “I mean, I think that anything is possible at this juncture.”
WATCH:
Transcript:
Karl: we’re almost out of time, but get to your future. I’m sure you saw the poll in New Hampshire that had you as the leading candidate, leading choice for Democrats. First, are you going to run for president?
Ocasio-Cortez: I mean, I’m focused on winning the midterms. I’m running for Congress right now.
Karl: But, I mean, do you see this as something? I mean, I know you said you’re open to it.
Ocasio-Cortez: Yes, I —
Karl: Is it a realistic possibility for you?
Ocasio-Cortez: I haven’t — well, I haven’t ruled out the possibility. And I’m very humbled to the tremendous amount of support out there. I think that we have a responsibility to remain focused on the midterms and not on our individual aspirations or plans.
Karl: And running for Senate against Chuck Schumer. Is that also something that’s possible?
Ocasio-Cortez: I mean, I think that anything is possible at this juncture.
The embattled Senate Minority Leader, Chuck Schumer, is likely on his way out as the Democratic Socialists of America gain steam in the Democratic Party.
Meanwhile, he has repeatedly dodged questions about the DSA’s growing influence and refused to say whether he would support DSA candidates even in the general election.
As The Gateway Pundit reported, Schumer last week dodged questions about Socialist Democratic Senate Nominee Abdul El-Sayed and the DSA ahead of the Michigan primary elections, where El-Sayed beat Schumer-backed Haley Stevens.

sources.news_title: AOC blames 2020 lockdown 'rhetoric' for past 'defund the police' support
sources.text:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) suggested the “rhetoric” seen during the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in 2020 was to blame for her past support of the “defund the police” movement.
“During this time and especially during COVID, there was a huge opening of the Overton window,” she said on ABC’s This Week on Sunday. “We were shut down. There were some of the highest unemployment rates that we have seen because of those shutdowns.”
Recommended Stories
“The doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place,” she added, “and I actually think that the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful.”
Ocasio-Cortez went on to say that talking about crime today is “fundamentally different” than talking about crime in 2020 and the years leading up to it, when criticism of police brutality was at an all-time high following several high-profile police-involved shootings.
“Of course, rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today,” she said.
Before Ocasio-Cortez gave her response, ABC News host Jonathan Karl cited her prior support of defunding the police as an example of whether the Left went too far after 2020. The progressive lawmaker has since moved away from her anti-police stance.
Karl brought up the issue because Wisconsin state Rep. Francesca Hong, a socialist running in the state’s Democratic primary for governor on Tuesday, called for abolishing prisons and police on social media from 2020 to 2021. She has since changed her position, now saying her focus is on strengthening public safety and addressing the root causes of crime instead of defunding the police.
Notably, Ocasio-Cortez has not endorsed Hong for governor because her focus is on “winning back” Congress for the midterm elections. The House Democrat has endorsed multiple congressional candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America.
AOC SAYS SHE HASN’T ‘RULED OUT THE POSSIBILITY’ OF 2028 PRESIDENTIAL BID
“I’m grateful that these candidates have the opportunity to present who they are to their electorate and what they’re campaigning on in this moment,” she said.
During the interview, Ocasio-Cortez invoked a saying used by socialist New York City Councilman Chi Osse: “Woke 1 was crazy.” The phrase references past policy positions taken by left-wing politicians during the early months of the pandemic and at the height of Black Lives Matter.

sources.news_title: Ocasio-Cortez hasn't 'ruled out' running for president or Senate in 2028
sources.text:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said Sunday she has not "ruled out" a run for president in 2028 as the Democratic Party's left flank surges in midterm primaries across the country.
"I haven't ruled out the possibility, and I'm very humbled [by] the tremendous amount of support out there," Ocasio-Cortez said when asked about a potential run on ABC's "This Week." "I think that we have a responsibility to remain focused on the midterms and not on our individual aspirations."
The New York Democrat, who has represented parts of the Bronx and Queens since 2019, has emerged as a polling favorite in key states ahead of the 2026 midterms. She has also become a power broker on the left, criss-crossing the country with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who came up short in the last two presidential primaries.
A recent poll from the University of New Hampshire found Ocasio-Cortez leading the field in the Granite State, ahead of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz.
Ocasio-Cortez also did not rule out a potential run for Senate in 2028, when Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is up for reelection.
"I think that anything is possible at this juncture," she said.
